text.p: Malaysian national car maker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton) should double its net profit for the year to March 31, 1997, based on a rise in production and a weaker yen, analysts said on Tuesday.

A poll of 33 analysts by Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimates Directory covering the stock, projected the company's net profit for the period to be 713 million ringgit ($282.9 million), compared to 354 million ringgit for the same period in 1996.
Earnings per share would jump from 69.7 cents per share in 1996 to 133 cents, according to the directory. Proton is expected to release its results this month.
"I'm expecting net profits to be around 707 million ringgit," said Corinna Cheah, automotive analyst at ING Barings in Kuala Lumpur.
"I'm basing this on the fact that production capacity has grown from 150,000 units per year to 180,000 units, and the weaker yen year-on-year," she said.
The yen has depreciated around 16 percent against the ringgit over the year to March 31, 1997.
Even though nearly 70 percent of the components are made locally, around 60 percent of the cost of making a Proton car is based on imported components.

This is because the company still has to import expensive items such as the engine and transmission systems from Japan. Consequently, Proton is very exposed to currency fluctuations, especially against the yen.
Most analysts currently have 'buy' recommendations on the stock.
But even though the current year's growth is likely to be spectacular, pressures on margins will begin to appear during the next few years, analysts said.

The completion of a new production plant in 1999 near the northern town of Tanjung Malim would boost production capacity to around 300,000 units initially, and ultimately to nearly 500,000, they said.
"The domestic market is unlikely to absorb all the new capacity, so Proton will have to look to the export markets," Cheah said.
Proton is currently protected from competition on home soil by the presence of tariffs on imported cars, reaching a maximum of around 200 percent.
Even more worrying for the company is the advent of the ASEAN Free Trade Area in 2003, which will see tariffs slashed on a range of consumer goods and services around the region.
"Proton is going to have to compete in the international market. If it is going to do this, it is going to have to cut its costs," said Choo Swee Kee, automotive analyst at brokers Vickers Ballas.
This will inevitably put pressure on margins, analysts said.
"Another factor is that Proton does not have brand recognition, the way Toyota has," said Chung Yee Wah, automotive analyst at HSBC James Capel.

One possible way for the company to attain such recognition would be for it to develop its own engine. The acquisition of ailing British sports car maker Group Lotus late in 1996 was largely seen as a way for Proton to buy the technological expertise it lacked to develop an engine.
Proton was unlikely to have its own engines for at least another five or six years, Cheah said.
However, with the potential development costs being extremely high, the wisdom of such a venture may itself be questionable, she said.
Proton shares closed on Tuesday at 12.90 ringgit, down 50 cents on the day.
($1 = 2.52 ringgit) -- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
